content.content:
1	Okay, so in the projects folder under CFFG, there is a pair of notes that are basically just articles written by my friend Magnus describing a machine learning system that is an undirected Bayesian network, which could be used as a platform for building active inference agents that do continuous learning.
2	
3	There's a lot of things one would want to do with such a system, and it could, I think, operate as an important system on its own or as a module in a larger learning system.  I think it's wonderful that this information was made publicly available, and I would love to try to get a coding agent to implement it. 
4	
5	The core idea that I would try to explore is we want to implement this in JAX and take inspiration from the way that the PGMax library allocates tensors. My understanding is that this approach to factor graphs described in the paper basically enables the combination of different message-passing algorithms to be used at different points in the graph, and that message-passing can basically just iterate for as many times as one wants, and the scheduling is an aspect of it, but it doesn't need to be overthought.
6	
7	We should be able to basically just pass messages until the system coheres. There also need to be constraints which can be set, and those constraints play a number of different roles. For example, the constraints can be priors on a distribution, the constraints can be a goal that the agent wants to fulfill, the constraints can be sensor information, etc. 
8	
9	Here is an assorted list of features that I would like to come with this implementation.
10	
11	1. there needs to be a serialization format that allows any CFFG to be described, and that format basically can act as a template which can be used to compose or construct more specific CFFG instances based upon that template. So the way that it should be constructed is that the CFFG contains the structure of the model in its entire specification except for the data that actually goes into the distributions. So any large blob data should be referred to as a file path, which can be accessed locally.
12	2.  The CFFG is going to have to be unrolled at certain points, and there will have to be some facility for unrolling it. We're going to want to enable rollouts, and the engine executing the CFFG should be designed to enable rollouts and different kinds of inference, such as backwards inference, forward planning, what-if analysis, and so on.
13	3.  the architecture should decouple what needs to be decoupled in order to facilitate a full model lifecycle. So eventually what we're going to want is a GUI interface for editing models, importing model templates and composing them, and then basically using data to set the distributions of those models, using data to create the structure of those models, and data is interpreted very broadly here because there are all kinds of data that an agent might want to bring to bear. So we need some kind of interface for working with data and mapping onto data as a pipeline so that this CFFG can interface with sensors and APIs for producing actions.  in addition to editing models, we are going to need to actually execute those models in the JAX engine using the backends that JAX provides, and be able to feed data in live and get actions and inferences out. And we need to be able to enable continual learning so that at every time step, the CFFG can be updated, and then at the end of a session or at any point in the session, we should be able to save the model data to disk so that as we train, we can incrementally get updated versions of the model 
14	4. The serialization format needs to enable incremental changes to the model so that when you want to make edits as a human user, things that need to change together are going to change together. This ensures that there are no dangling edges in the model, and any dangling edges at runtime are going to be filled with something, whether that is incoming data or a goal that the user has already specified in the general or specific case, or also just solving dangling edges by gluing together the next step of the rollout, and so on and so forth. So probably for action models, there will need to be like a way to specify that there is a point where the model is going to be glued together with the next stage of the rollout. 
15	5. we're going to want a test suite for these factor graphs, which tests a couple of different facilities. One would be like tasks which are undirected, namely some kind of constraint satisfaction problem, and then there are going to be tasks which are sequential inference problems where you simply have to predict what the system is going to do next, and then third, there's going to be action models where you have a sequence model that actually needs to fulfill its curiosity and select an action that is going to reduce its free energy.  for each of these facilities, we're going to need a sort of canonical test where we know exactly what the underlying environment is, and we can see how well the model is converging to a true world model. 
16	6.  Eventually, we are going to want a GUI. For this first stage, let's not have a GUI, but we need to have the serialization layer and the sort of API for editing models be made with a GUI in mind, so that again, we can enable edit actions, which comprise a bundle of changes to the model that are basically going to result in a valid model.
17	7.  we're going to need a tool for estimating how much computational resource will be needed to run the model on the given hardware. This can be somewhat approximate, but there should be a way to sort of, you know, fit a curve, if nothing else, that will predict how much memory is going to be needed and how much CPU time or something it's going to take to run a step of the model. 
18	8.  if the serialization format is compatible with or mappable into ONNX model formats, that would be really good.  if we can take advantage of existing probabilistic libraries on the back end, that would also be good, but we need to make sure that we are achieving true BFE for the free energy and not taking shortcuts.
19	9.

Realising Synthetic Active Inference Agents,
Part I: Epistemic Objectives and Graphical
Specification Language
Magnus Koudahl1,2 , Thijs van de Laar1 , and Bert de Vries1,3
1

BIASLab, Department of Electrical Engineering, Eindhoven
University of Technology, The Netherlands
2

3

Netherlands
October 17, 2023
Abstract
The Free Energy Principle (FEP) is a theoretical framework for describing how (intelligent) systems self-organise into coherent, stable structures by minimising a free energy functional. Active Inference (AIF) is a
corollary of the FEP that specifically details how systems that are able to
plan for the future (agents) function by minimising particular free energy
functionals that incorporate information seeking components. This paper
is the first in a series of two where we derive a synthetic version of AIF
on free form factor graphs. The present paper focuses on deriving a local
version of the free energy functionals used for AIF. This enables us to
construct a version of AIF which applies to arbitrary graphical models
and interfaces with prior work on message passing (MP) algorithms. The
resulting messages are derived in our companion paper. We also identify a
gap in the graphical notation used for factor graphs. While factor graphs
are great at expressing a generative model, they have so far been unable
to specify the full optimisation problem including constraints. To solve
this problem we develop constrained Forney-style factor graph (CFFG)
notation which permits a fully graphical description of variational inference objectives. We then proceed to show how CFFGs can be used to
reconstruct prior algorithms for AIF as well as derive new ones. The
latter is demonstrated by deriving an algorithm that permits direct policy inference for AIF agents, circumventing a long standing scaling issue
that has so far hindered the application of AIF in industrial settings. We
demonstrate our algorithm on the classic T-maze task and show that it
reproduces the information seeking behaviour that is a hallmark feature
of AIF.

44	Introduction
45	
46	Active Inference (AIF) is an emerging framework for modelling intelligent agents
47	interacting with an environment. Originating in the ﬁeld of computational neuroscience, it has since been spread to numerous other ﬁelds such as modern
48	machine learning. At its core, AIF relies on variational inference techniques
49	to minimise a free energy functional. A key diﬀerentiator of AIF compared to
50	other approaches is the use of custom free energy functionals such as Expected
51	and Generalised free energies (expected free energy (EFE) and generalised free
52	energy (GFE), respectively). These functionals are speciﬁcally constructed so
53	as to elicit epistemic, information-seeking behaviour when used to infer actions.
54	Optimisation of these functionals have so far relied on custom algorithms
55	that require evaluating very large search trees which has rendered upscaling of
56	AIF diﬃcult. Many recent works, such as Branching Time AIF [3] and sophisticated inference [7] have investigated algorithmic ways to prune the search tree
57	in order to solve this problem.
58	This paper is the ﬁrst in a series of two parts where we take a diﬀerent
59	approach and formulate a variation of the GFE optimisation problem using
60	a custom Lagrangian derived from constrained Bethe free energy (CBFE) on
61	factor graphs. Using variational calculus we then derive a custom MP algorithm
62	that can directly solve for ﬁxed points of local GFE terms, removing the need for
63	a search tree. This allows us to construct a purely optimisation-based approach
64	to AIF which we name Lagrangian Active Inference (LAIF).
65	LAIF applies to arbitrary graph topologies and interfaces with generic MP
66	algorithms which allow for scaling up of AIF using oﬀ-the-shelf tools. We accomplish this by constructing a node-local GFE on generic factor graphs.
67	The present paper is structured as follows: In section 2, we review relevant
68	background material concerning Forney-style factor graphs (FFGs) and Bethe
69	free energy (BFE). In section 3 we formalise what we mean by "epistemics" and
70	construct an objective that is local to a single node on an FFG and possesses
71	an epistemic, information-seeking drive. This objective turns out to be a local
72	version of the GFE which we review in section 3.2.
73	Once we start modifying the free energy functional, we recognise a problem with current FFG notation. FFGs visualise generative models but fail to
74	display a signiﬁcant part of the optimisation problem, namely, the variational
75	distribution and the functional to be optimised.
76	To remedy this, we develop the CFFG graphical notation in section 5 as a
77	method for visualising both the variational distribution and any adaptations to
78	the free energy functional that are needed for AIF. These tools form the basis
79	of the update rules derived in our companion paper [15].
80	With the CFFG notation in hand, in section 6 we then proceed to demonstrate how to recover prior algorithms for AIF as MP on a CFFG. AIF is often
81	described as MP on a probabilistic graphical model, see [4, 6, 13, 26] for examples. However, this relationship has not been properly formalised before, in part
82	because adequate notation has been lacking. Using CFFGs it is straightforward
83	to accurately write down this relation. Further, due to the modular nature of
84	2
85	
86	 CFFGs it becomes easy to devise extensions to prior AIF algorithms that can
87	be implemented using oﬀ-the-shelf MP tools.
88	Finally, section 7 demonstrates a new algorithm for policy inference using
89	LAIF that scales linearly in the planning horizon, providing a solution to a longstanding barrier for scaling AIF to larger models and more complex tasks.

96	objectives.
97	As a free energy functional, the BFE is unique because stationary points of
98	the BFE correspond to solutions of the belief propagation algorithm [20, 25, 28]
99	which provides exact inference on tree-structured graphs.
100	Furthermore, by adding constraints to the BFE using Lagrange multipliers,
101	one can form a custom Lagrangian for an inference problem. Taking the ﬁrst
102	variation of this Lagrangian, one can then solve for stationary points and obtain
103	MP algorithms that solve the desired problem. Prior work [25, 28] have shown
104	that adding additional constraints to the BFE allows for deriving a host of different message passing algorithms including variational message passing (VMP)
105	[27] and expectation propagation (EP) [18] among others. We refer interested
106	readers to [25] for a comprehensive overview of this technique and how diﬀerent
107	choices of constraints can lead to diﬀerent algorithms.
108	Constraints are speciﬁed at the level of nodes and edges, meaning this procedure can produce hybrid MP algorithms, foreshadowing the approach we are
109	going to take for deriving a local, epistemic objective for AIF.

Introduction

interacting with an environment. Originating in the ﬁeld of computational neuroscience, it has since been spread to numerous other ﬁelds such as modern
machine learning. At its core, AIF relies on variational inference techniques
to minimise a free energy functional. A key diﬀerentiator of AIF compared to
other approaches is the use of custom free energy functionals such as Expected
and Generalised free energies (expected free energy (EFE) and generalised free
energy (GFE), respectively). These functionals are speciﬁcally constructed so
as to elicit epistemic, information-seeking behaviour when used to infer actions.
Optimisation of these functionals have so far relied on custom algorithms
that require evaluating very large search trees which has rendered upscaling of
AIF diﬃcult. Many recent works, such as Branching Time AIF [3] and sophisticated inference [7] have investigated algorithmic ways to prune the search tree
in order to solve this problem.
This paper is the ﬁrst in a series of two parts where we take a diﬀerent
approach and formulate a variation of the GFE optimisation problem using
a custom Lagrangian derived from constrained Bethe free energy (CBFE) on
factor graphs. Using variational calculus we then derive a custom MP algorithm
that can directly solve for ﬁxed points of local GFE terms, removing the need for
a search tree. This allows us to construct a purely optimisation-based approach
to AIF which we name Lagrangian Active Inference (LAIF).
LAIF applies to arbitrary graph topologies and interfaces with generic MP
algorithms which allow for scaling up of AIF using oﬀ-the-shelf tools. We accomplish this by constructing a node-local GFE on generic factor graphs.
The present paper is structured as follows: In section 2, we review relevant
background material concerning Forney-style factor graphs (FFGs) and Bethe

construct an objective that is local to a single node on an FFG and possesses

version of the GFE which we review in section 3.2.

display a signiﬁcant part of the optimisation problem, namely, the variational

3

Defining epistemic objectives

Now we move on to the central topic of AIF, namely agents that interact with
the world they inhabit. Under the heading of AIF, an agent entails a generative
model of its environment and is engaged in the process of achieving future goals
(speciﬁed by a target distribution or goal prior) through actions. This task can
be cast as a process of free energy minimisation [5, 7, 8]. A natural question to
ask is then, what should this free energy functional look like and why? Here we
wish to highlight a core feature of AIF that sets it apart from other approaches:
Systematic information gathering by targeted exploration of an environment.
Whatever the form of our free energy functional, it should lead to agents that
possess an exploratory drive consistent with AIF.
While it is tempting to default to a standard VFE, prior work [24] has
shown that directly optimising BFE or VFE when inferring a sequence of actions
(which we will refer to as a policy) does not lead to agents that systematically
explore their environment. Instead, directly inferring a policy by minimising a
VFE/BFE leads to Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL)-control [12] 1 . This means
that VFE/BFE is not the correct choice when we desire an agent that actively
samples its environment with the explicit purpose of gathering information.
Instead a hallmark feature of AIF is the use of alternative functionals in
place of either the VFE or the BFE, speciﬁcally for inferring policies. The
goal of these alternative functionals is often speciﬁcally to induce an epistemic,
explorative term that drives AIF agents to seek out information.
1 Other works will sometimes use π as a symbol to denote a policy

6

 Epistemics, epistemic behaviour or "foraging for information" are commonly
used terms in the AIF literature and related ﬁelds. While we have used the term
colloquially until this point, we now clarify formally how we use the term in the
present paper and how it relates to the objective functionals we consider. A
core problem is that epistemics is most often deﬁned in terms of the behaviour
of agents ("what does my agent do?") rather than from a mathematical point
of view. Prior work on this point includes [10, 17].
We take the view that epistemics arise from the optimisation of either an mutual information (MI) term or a bound thereon. The MI (between two variables
x and z) is deﬁned as [16]

key insight is that messages ﬂowing out of P derived from stationary points of
Eq. (25) will correspond to stationary points of the local GFE rather than BFE,
meaning the result will include an epistemic component. This paves the way for
a localised version of AIF that applies to arbitrary graph structures, does not
suﬀer from scaling issues as the planning horizon increases, and can be solved
eﬃciently and asynchronously using MP.

5

Constrained Forney-style factor graphs

While FFGs are a useful tool for writing down generative models, we have by
now established the importance of knowing the exact functional to be minimised.
This requires specifying not just the model f but also the family Q through
constraints and any potential P-substitutions. This is important if we want to
be able to succinctly specify not just the model but also the exact inference
problem we aim to solve.
We will now develop just such a new notation for writing constraints directly
as part of the FFG. We refer to FFGs with added constraints speciﬁcation as
CFFGs.

Figure 3: An example FFG.
Fig 3 shows a model comprised of ﬁve edges and six nodes. FFGs traditionally represent the model f using squares connected by lines as shown in Fig. 3.
The squares represent factors and the connections between them represent variables. Connecting an edge to a square node indicates that the variable on that
edge is an argument of the factor it is connected to.
The notation for CFFGs adheres to similar principles when specifying f .
However, we augment the FFG with circular beads to indicate the constraints
that deﬁne our family Q. Each factor of the variational distribution in q will
correspond to a bead and the position of a bead indicates to which marginal
it refers - a bead on an edge denotes an edge marginal q(si ) and a bead inside
a node denotes a node marginal q(sa ). An empty bead will denote the default
normalisation constraints while a connection between beads indicates marginalisation constraints following Eq. (9). These beads form the basic building blocks
of our notation.

2436	Conclusions
2437	
2438	In this paper we have proposed a novel approach to AIF based on lagrangian
2439	optimisation which we have named Lagrangian Active Inference (LAIF). We
2440	demonstrated LAIF on a classic benchmark problem from the AIF literature
2441	and found that it inherits the epistemic drive that is a hallmark feature of AIF.
2442	LAIF presents three main advantages over previous algorithms for AIF.
2443	Firstly, an advantage of LAIF is the computational eﬃciency aﬀorded by
2444	being able to pass backward messages instead of needing to perform forwards
2445	rollouts for every policy. While LAIF is still an iterative procedure, the computational complexity of each iteration scales linearly in the size of the planning
2446	horizon T instead of exponentially.
2447	A second advantage is that LAIF allows for directly inferring posteriors
2448	over control signals instead of relying on a model comparison step based on
2449	EFE/GFE. This means that LAIF uniﬁes inference for perception, learning,

Fig. 30 once again shows that the agent is able to infer the optimal policy for
solving the task. For repeated runs, the agent will randomly select to move to
either position 2 or 3 at the second step due to minute diﬀerences in the Monte
Carlo estimates used for computing the messages. The pointmass constraint
obscures this since it forces the marginal to put all mass on the MAP estimate.
37

 The point of repeating the experiments with δ-constraints is not to show
that the behaviour of the agent changes dramatically. Instead, the idea is to
demonstrate that CFFGs allow for modular speciﬁcation of AIF agents which
allows for adapting parts of the model without having to touch the rest. In
this case, the only parts of inference that change are those involving the control
marginal. This means all messages out of the P-substituted composite nodes
are unaﬀected since the δ-constraints are only applied to the control marginals.

8

Conclusions

In this paper we have proposed a novel approach to AIF based on lagrangian
optimisation which we have named Lagrangian Active Inference (LAIF). We
demonstrated LAIF on a classic benchmark problem from the AIF literature
and found that it inherits the epistemic drive that is a hallmark feature of AIF.
LAIF presents three main advantages over previous algorithms for AIF.
Firstly, an advantage of LAIF is the computational eﬃciency aﬀorded by
being able to pass backward messages instead of needing to perform forwards
rollouts for every policy. While LAIF is still an iterative procedure, the computational complexity of each iteration scales linearly in the size of the planning
horizon T instead of exponentially.
A second advantage is that LAIF allows for directly inferring posteriors
over control signals instead of relying on a model comparison step based on
EFE/GFE. This means that LAIF uniﬁes inference for perception, learning,
and actions into a single procedure without any overhead - it all becomes part
of the same inference procedure. See our companion paper [15] for more details.
Thirdly, LAIF is inherently modular and consequently works for freely deﬁnable CFFGs, while prior work has focused mostly on speciﬁc generative models.
Extensions to hierarchical or heterarchical models are straightforward and only
require writing out the corresponding CFFG.
We have also introduced CFFG notation for writing down constraints and
P-subtitutions on an FFG. CFFGs are useful not just for AIF but for specifying
free energy functionals in general. CFFGs accomplish this through a simple
and intuitive graphical syntax. Our hope is that CFFGs can become a standard
tool similar to FFGs when it is desirable to write not just a model f but also
a family of approximating distributions Q. Speciﬁcally in the context of AIF
we have also introduced P-substitution as a way to modify the underlying free
energy functional. In doing so we have formalised the relation between AIF and
message passing on a CFFG, paving the way for future developments.
In future work, we plan to extend LAIF to more node constructions to further
open up the scope of available problems that can be attacked using AIF.

4

General GFE-Based Message Updates

In the model for future states, the goal prior and observation model impose simultaneous
constraints on the observation variable. In the corresponding CFFG, this configuration
is modelled by two facing nodes. In this section we derive the general GFE-based
message updates for a pair of facing nodes. We express the local optimisation problem
as a Lagrangian. Using variational calculus we then derive local stationary solutions,
from which we obtain general update expressions for GFE-based messages.

4.1

Goal and Observation Model

Here we define a generalised goal and observation model, which define simultaneous
constraints on the observation variable x. The observation model p(x|z, θ) consists
of states z and parameters θ. The goal prior extends to a goal model p̃(x|w, ϕ), with
states w and parameters ϕ, expanding the range of applicability.
The CFFG of Fig. 4 draws the observation and goal model as two facing nodes.
Crucially, from the perspective of the CFFG the role of these nodes in the bigger model
is irrelevant, expanding the range of applicability beyond observation and goal models.
Moreover, the facing nodes are contained by a composite structure that acts as a Markov
blanket for communication with the remaining graph.

While direct application of (19) works well in some cases, this message update may
also yield algorithms for which the GFE actually diverges over iterations. This perhaps

theorems. While our theorems prove that the stationary messages correspond to fixedpoints of the node-local Lagrangian, the theorems do not guarantee that iterations of
the fixed-point equations actually converge to said fixed-points. In order to improve

1640	The Forney-style Factor Graph (FFG) notation was first introduced by (Forney, 2001).
1641	The work of (Loeliger, 2007) offers a comprehensive introduction to message passing

1646	2005) and formulated in the context of FFGs by (Dauwels, 2007). A more recent view on
1647	constrained free energy optimisation can be found in (Zhang et al., 2017). Furthermore,
1648	(Şenöz et al., 2021) offers a comprehensive overview of common constraints and
1649	resulting message passing updates on factor graphs.

1651	2019) proposed a Generalised Free Energy (GFE) objective, which incorporates prior

1653	reformulates these ideas in a visual CFFG framework, which explicates the role of

To illustrate the scalability of our approach, a second extension modifies the T-maze
simulation to a multi-agent bargaining setting, where a primary agent (the buyer) purchases its cue (indicating the reward position) from a secondary agent (the seller). The
buyer navigates the T-maze and can only access the cue through the seller. Conversely,
the seller can only access reward through the buyer. The currency of their exchange is
the reward probability αs , set by the seller for each trial s. By visiting the cue position
C, the buyer (primary agent) agrees to pay the seller (secondary agent) a share 1 − αs
of the reward probability, leaving αs for the buyer. The price is determined by the seller
from a set of L potential offers αs ∈ A. If the buyer (primary agent) chooses to avoid
C (forfeiting the cue) then the seller receives nothing and the buyer receives the full
share (αs = 1) if the reward is obtained.
We extend the state variable zk of the buyer (navigating the T-maze) with a bargain
state C = (CV, NC), indicating the respective acceptance and rejection of the seller’s
offer. The buyer’s state then becomes zk ∈ C × P × R. The buyer then starts each
simulation trial in an NC bargain state,

8

Related Work

The Forney-style Factor Graph (FFG) notation was first introduced by (Forney, 2001).
The work of (Loeliger, 2007) offers a comprehensive introduction to message passing
on FFGs in the context of signal processing and estimation.
The belief propagation algorithm was pioneered by (Pearl, 1982), and was further
formalised in terms of variational optimisation by (Kschischang et al., 2001; Yedidia
et al., 2001). Variational Message Passing (VMP) was introduced by (Winn and Bishop,
2005) and formulated in the context of FFGs by (Dauwels, 2007). A more recent view on
constrained free energy optimisation can be found in (Zhang et al., 2017). Furthermore,
(Şenöz et al., 2021) offers a comprehensive overview of common constraints and
resulting message passing updates on factor graphs.
Towards a message passing formulation of Active Inference (AIF), (Parr and Friston,
2019) proposed a Generalised Free Energy (GFE) objective, which incorporates prior
beliefs on future outcomes as part of the Generative Model (GM). The current paper
reformulates these ideas in a visual CFFG framework, which explicates the role of
backward messages in GFE optimisation (see also our companion paper (Koudahl et al.,
2023)). Inspired by (Winn and Bishop, 2005), prior work by (Champion et al., 2021)
derives variational message passing updates for AIF by augmenting variational message
updates with an Expected Free Energy (EFE) term. In contrast, the current paper takes
a constrained optimisation approach, augmenting the variational objective itself, and
deriving message update expressions by variational optimisation.
Message passing formulations of AIF allow for modular extension to hierarchical
structures. Temporal thickness in the context of message passing is explored by (de Vries
and Friston, 2017), which formulates deep temporal AIF by message passing on an
FFG representation of a hierarchical GM. Implications of message passing in deep
temporal models on neural connectivity are further explored by (Friston et al., 2017).
An operational framework and simulation environment for AIF by message passing on
FFGs is described by (van de Laar and de Vries, 2019).
Concerning epistemics and the exploration-exploitation trade-off, the pioneering
work of (Friston et al., 2015) formally decomposes an EFE objective in constituent
drivers for behaviour, and motivates epistemic value from the perspective of maximizing
26

 information gain. A detailed view by (Koudahl et al., 2021) considers EFE minimisation
in the context of linear Gaussian dynamical systems, and shows that AIF does not lead
to purposeful explorative behaviour in this context.
Unfortunately, as our companion paper argues, the EFE optimisation viewpoint
does not readily extend to message passing on free-form models (Koudahl et al., 2023).
Towards resolving this limitation, (Schwöbel et al., 2018) formulated AIF as BFE optimisation, but also notes that the BFE lacks the crucial ambiguity-reducing component
of the EFE that induces exploration. An alternative objective, the free energy of the
expected future, was introduced by (Millidge et al., 2020). This objective includes the
ambiguity-reducing component of the EFE and can be interpreted as the divergence from
a biased to a veridical GM. An alternative AIF objective was proposed by (van de Laar
et al., 2022), which considers epistemic behaviour from a constrained BFE perspective.
A biologically plausible view on message passing for AIF is described by (Parr
et al., 2019), which combines the strengths of belief propagation and VMP to describe
an alternative type of marginal message update.

9

Conclusions

This paper has taken a constraint-centric approach to synthetic Active Inference (AIF),
and simulated a perception-action cycle through message passing derived from a single
Generalised Free Energy (GFE) objective. Specifically, we have used a Constrained
Forney-style Factor Graph (CFFG) visual representation to distinguish between the
Generative Model (GM) and constraints on the Variational Free Energy (VFE).
Through constraint visualisations we have shown how the free energy objectives for
perception, control and learning for AIF can be unified under a single GM specification
and schedule, with time-dependent constraints.
The impact of our contributions lies with a modular and scalable formulation of
synthetic AIF agents. Using variational calculus, we have derived general message
update rules for GFE-based control. This allows for a modular approach to synthetic
AIF, where custom message updates can be derived and reused across models (Cox
et al., 2019). As an example we have derived GFE-based messages for a general
configuration of two facing nodes, and applied these results to derive specific messages
for a discrete-variable goal-observation submodel that is often used in AIF practice.
The general update rules allow for deriving GFE-based messages around alternative
sub-models, including continuous-variable models and possibly chance-constrained
models (van de Laar et al., 2021). Additionally, the general message update results
allow for a parametrised goal prior, which may me modelled by a secondary dynamical
model (Sennesh et al., 2022).
Crucially, the local updates include novel backward messages that have not been

unified optimisation of the full GFE objective, without resorting to distinct schedules for

# AGENTS.md — Ground Rules for the CFFG Project

This repository implements **Constrained Forney-style Factor Graphs (CFFGs)** and
**Lagrangian Active Inference (LAIF)** in JAX, following:

- *Realising Synthetic Active Inference Agents, Part I: Epistemic Objectives and
  Graphical Specification Language* (Koudahl, van de Laar, de Vries — arXiv:2306.08014)
- *Part II: Variational Message Updates* (van de Laar, Koudahl, de Vries)

Both papers live in `notes/` (PDFs plus extracted text). The project brief is in the
Obsidian vault at `agents/CFFG/0.0.md`. Reference implementation for parity testing:
https://github.com/biaslab/LAIF (Julia/RxInfer).

## Rules

1. **Package management: `uv` only.** Use `uv init`, `uv add`, `uv run`, `uv sync`.
   Never call `pip` directly, never hand-edit lockfiles. The venv is managed by uv.

2. **Atomic git commits.** One logical change per commit — a commit should build and
   pass tests on its own. Commit early and often; keep refactors separate from
   behavior changes. Reference ticket IDs in commit messages (e.g. `tk-42: ...`).

3. **Tickets via `tk`.** All work is tracked in the `tk` ticket system (`tk --help`
   for usage). Break work into small tickets with dependency links, use epics for the
   major milestones, and close tickets in the same session as the commit that
   resolves them. Before starting work, check `tk` for ready tickets.

4. **Act autonomously.** The agent has broad access to this machine and should use
   it: run tests, install deps, create tickets, commit, and keep moving without
   asking for permission on routine steps. Ask only for genuinely irreversible or
   scope-changing decisions.

5. **Side research goes to sub-agents.** When background reading is needed
   (downloading another paper, checking how PGMax allocates tensors, clarifying an
   active-inference derivation), spawn a sub-agent with the *specific questions* to
   answer and have it report back a short summary. Do not read whole papers into the
   main context window mid-task.

## Technical invariants

- **True Bethe/Generalised free energy.** No shortcuts in the objective: free-energy
  evaluation must follow the papers' definitions (node-local BFE terms, edge-entropy
  overcounting corrections, P-substitution for GFE nodes). FE values are the
  convergence signal and the policy-scoring quantity — treat them as first-class
  outputs, and test them against analytically known cases.
- **Messages in log-space** wherever feasible; normalize aggressively; explicit JAX
  PRNG keys for anything stochastic (e.g. importance-sampled messages) so runs are
  reproducible.
- **Serialization is the source of truth.** Model structure lives in the template
  format (no large blobs inline — blobs are file paths); the compiled JAX arena is a
  derived artifact and must always be reconstructible from the template + data.

# CFFG Engine — Architecture Plan

Status: proposal, 2026-07-05. Sources: Koudahl et al. Part I (arXiv:2306.08014),
van de Laar et al. Part II, project brief in Obsidian `agents/CFFG/0.0.md`.

## What the papers give us (and what they don't)

The papers provide a complete recipe for a specific, powerful thing:

- **CFFG notation**: a factor graph (nodes = factors, edges = variables) *plus
  constraint annotations* ("beads") that fully specify the variational optimization
  problem — factorization constraints, form constraints (δ/pointmass, etc.),
  moment-matching constraints, and **P-substitution** (replace `q(x)` with
  `p(x|z,θ)` in a node-local expectation, turning that node's local VFE into a local
  **Generalised Free Energy** with an epistemic mutual-information term).
- **Hybrid message passing**: constraints are node/edge-local, so different
  algorithms (BP, VMP, EP, GFE-messages) coexist on one graph. Stationary points of
  the constrained Bethe Lagrangian = fixed points of message passing.
- **Closed-form GFE messages for the discrete goal-observation submodel**
  (Cat/Dirichlet): Part II Fig. 5 gives the message table. Two are nontrivial:
  the backward state message is found by solving `z̄ = σ(ρ(z̄) + log d)` with
  Newton's method (the naive fixed-point update can diverge — Part II §4.5), and
  the message to the observation matrix A is a non-standard log-message evaluated
  by importance sampling (making GFE evaluation stochastic; average after burn-in).
- **A validation target**: T-maze results (policy posteriors in Part I Fig. 28,
  learning curves in Part II §7) plus the biaslab/LAIF Julia reference code.

What they do *not* give: GFE messages for arbitrary node types. Each new
factor-type × constraint combination needs a derived update rule. So the engine
must be organized around an **extensible rule registry**, not a universal solver.

## Layered design

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 5. Agent runtime   perception-action loop, rolling      │
│                    horizon, continual learning, ckpts   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 4. Inference VM    schedules, damping, FE accounting,   │
│                    convergence monitoring               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. Rule library    per (factor-type, constraint-config) │
│                    message updates: BP / VMP / GFE      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. Compiler        template → grounded graph → arenas   │
│                    (PGMax-style) → jitted step function │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. Core IR         typed CFFG graph + constraints +     │
│                    ports; serialization; edit actions   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 1. Core IR and serialization (`cffg.core`)

A pure-Python (dataclass) representation, independent of JAX:

- `VariableSpec` (domain: categorical cardinality now, continuous later),
  `FactorSpec` (type + parameter refs), `ConstraintSpec` (bead types:
  normalization, marginalization, form/δ, moment-matching, P-substitution set 𝒫),
  `CompositeNode` (Markov-blanket grouping, e.g. the goal-observation pair).
- **Templates with ports.** A template is a CFFG fragment whose boundary edges are
  declared **ports** with roles: `data` (sensor clamp), `goal` (goal prior),
  `prior` (parameter prior), `glue` (connects to the next unrolled slice). A model
  is valid iff every port is terminated by data, a prior/goal, or a glue bond.
  This is the single mechanism behind unrolling, rollouts, "no dangling edges,"
  and composing templates — one invariant instead of four features.
- **Serialization**: versioned JSON (or msgpack) schema for structure and
  constraints; all array data (A matrices, Dirichlet counts, goal statistics)
  referenced as file paths to `safetensors`/`.npz` blobs. Content hash of the
  structural part keys the JIT cache.
- **Edit actions**: the only public mutation API is transactional bundles
  (`add_slice`, `bind_data`, `set_constraint`, `compose(template, port_map)`) that
  validate the port invariant before committing. This is the GUI-ready surface —
  a GUI later is just a client of this API, and edit actions double as an
  incremental (append-only) serialization of model history.

### 2. Compiler (`cffg.compile`)

Two-phase, mirroring PGMax:

1. **Grounding**: template + horizon + data bindings → flat grounded graph.
   Unrolling = repeated self-composition along glue ports. Time-dependent
   constraints applied here: past observation edges get δ (data) constraints,
   future observation edges get P-substitution + goal prior — this is exactly how
   the papers unify perception and planning in one model.

  log-message to A. All in log-space; every stochastic rule takes an explicit PRNG

  energy + entropy terms with correct edge-entropy overcounting), so global

  right that scheduling shouldn't be overthought — flooding + iterate-to-coherence

  constraint flips from goal to data δ), glue one new slice at the horizon,
  re-infer, read the control marginal (or its MAP under a δ-constraint), emit
  action. This directly fixes the hard-horizon problem the papers flag with the

1. **Undirected / CSP**: small Ising or Potts grids and a mini-Sudoku; check BP

  `p(x|z,θ)` in a node-local expectation, turning that node's local VFE into a local

Done — read your Obsidian brief and both papers cover to cover, committed `AGENTS.md` with your five ground rules, and wrote the full architecture plan to `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`. Two commits on `main` (I also set the repo's git identity to your email since the machine had none configured). Here's the plan and my honest take.

## What the papers actually hand us

This is a better-specified project than most paper implementations. Part I gives the CFFG notation — a factor graph plus constraint "beads" that fully specify the variational problem, where **P-substitution** (swapping `q(x)` for `p(x|z,θ)` inside one node's local expectation) turns that node's local Bethe free energy into a local *Generalised* free energy with the epistemic mutual-information term. Part II then derives the actual message updates, including closed-form ones for the discrete goal-observation submodel, and — importantly — reproduces the T-maze with published numbers we can test against, plus a Julia reference implementation (biaslab/LAIF).

What the papers **don't** give: GFE messages for arbitrary node types. Every new factor-type × constraint combo needs a derived rule. So the engine's spine is an **extensible message-rule registry**, not a universal solver — that framing drives the whole design.

## Architecture in five layers

1. **Core IR** — pure-Python typed graph + constraints, JAX-free. The key idea I'd add to your plan: **templates with typed ports**. Boundary edges declare a role — `data`, `goal`, `prior`, or `glue` — and a model is valid iff every port is terminated. That one invariant *is* your unrolling mechanism, your rollout gluing, your no-dangling-edges rule, and your template composition, unified. Edit actions are transactional bundles validated against it — that's the GUI-ready surface.
2. **Compiler** — template → grounded (unrolled) graph → PGMax-style flat tensor arenas with gather/scatter index maps → one jitted `lax.scan` step. Structure edits recompile; data edits don't.
3. **Rule library** — BP/VMP for standard nodes, the Part II Fig. 5 GFE messages for the P-substituted composite. Every rule ships with its local free-energy term, so global BFE/GFE is structurally guaranteed to be the true sum — your "no shortcuts" requirement enforced by construction.
4. **Inference VM** — flooding schedule, damping, per-node FE tracking. Your inference modes (filtering, planning, what-if, backward) are just constraint presets on the same grounded graph.
5. **Agent runtime** — receding-horizon loop: each tick flips one future edge's constraint from goal-prior to data-δ, glues a new slice at the horizon, re-infers, emits the control marginal. This directly fixes the hard-time-horizon problem the papers themselves flag.

## Where I'd amend your plan

- **You're right that scheduling isn't the hard part — but "iterate until it coheres" needs teeth.** Part II §4.5 explicitly shows the naive GFE fixed-point update can *diverge*; the fix is their Corollary 1 form solved with Newton's method (the paper uses ~20 steps). Also the message to the A matrix is importance-sampled, so the GFE is stochastic and needs burn-in averaging. Coherence must be a measured number (FE deltas), not a vibe.
- **ONNX: I'd drop it as a model format.** ONNX encodes directed NN operator graphs; it can't represent constraints or P-substitution without opaque custom ops — it'd be our format in a costume. The honest version of this goal: export the *compiled inference step* via StableHLO/jax2onnx for deployment. Model interchange stays our own schema.
- **Probabilistic libraries**: borrow PGMax's arena ideas by reading, not depending (it's BP-only), and use distrax/TFP only for distribution math. The FE accounting must be ours.
- **Discrete first.** All closed-form GFE messages in the papers are Cat/Dirichlet. Continuous/Gaussian GFE messages are genuinely new derivation work — schedule them as research, not engineering.
- **Add a BFE-ablation test**: flipping one constraint bead turns the epistemic agent into the non-epistemic baseline (Part II does exactly this). It's a beautiful regression test for the epistemic machinery — one-bit diff, dramatic behavioral difference.

Your three-tier test suite maps cleanly to milestones: CSP/Ising → HMM-vs-exact-forward-backward → T-maze parity against the published posteriors (≈[.20 .30 .30 .20] then [.25 .13 .35 .26]). And your resource estimator gets a concrete answer for free: post-compile shapes are static, so memory is analytic and `jax.jit(...).lower().compile().cost_analysis()` gives FLOPs — plus a small calibration fit per backend.

## Overall feelings

Genuinely enthusiastic. It's rare that an active-inference project comes with derived message tables, a divergence warning with its own fix, published golden numbers, and reference source code — Magnus and coauthors did the field a real service. The two risks worth respecting: importance-sampling noise in parameter learning (the paper's own Fig. 9 shows agents sometimes stuck in local optima — expect that, don't debug it as a defect), and scope creep on the rule registry (the "arbitrary graphs" promise is only as real as the rules we've derived). The port-based template design is the piece I'd defend hardest — it's what makes the GUI, the rollouts, and the serialization story one problem instead of four.

Next step when you're ready: M0 scaffolding — `uv init`, tk epics for M1–M6, pytest/ruff CI. Say the word and I'll start.

input.content:
# Known Limitations of the CFFG/LAIF Engine

Status: assessed 2026-07-05, before implementation. "Hard" = inherent to the
mathematical framework (constrained Bethe free energy + message passing + LAIF);
finishing the roadmap does not remove these. "Soft" = removable with additional
derivation or engineering work; each is a future research/engineering ticket.

## Hard limitations

**H1. Bethe is an approximation on loopy graphs.** Stationary points of the BFE
equal fixed points of belief propagation, and that is exact only on trees. On
loopy graphs marginals are approximate, the iteration may not converge, may
oscillate, or may converge to a wrong fixed point — and there is no general
certificate telling you which happened. Damping and good schedules mitigate;
nothing eliminates. Every interesting agent model (loops through time, shared
parameters) is loopy.

**H2. The posterior family is bounded by the constraint vocabulary.** Mean-field
and structured factorizations discard posterior correlations across beads by
construction. Strongly correlated or multimodal joint posteriors (explaining-away
between factorized variables, symmetric modes) cannot be represented, only
projected onto the chosen family. Richer constraints widen the family but the
principle stands: you choose the approximation when you draw the beads.

**H3. No structure learning inside the objective.** Continual learning updates
*parameters* (conjugate posterior → next prior). The graph topology, state-space
cardinalities, and factorization are fixed by the template. The framework has no
gradient that adds a latent variable, splits a state, or discovers a new factor.
(An outer loop scoring candidate structures by free energy is possible — see S6 —
but that is model *comparison* wrapped around the engine, not learning within it.)

**H4. Tabular representation → combinatorial state walls.** Discrete variables are
one-hot; joint states are Kronecker products. The T-maze is 4 positions × 2 reward
contexts = 8 states; every new orthogonal feature multiplies. A matrices are
|X|×|Z|, controlled transitions |Z|²×|U|. There is no representation learning and
no amortization: raw pixels, audio, or text cannot be consumed without a
hand-built (or externally learned) discretization/featurization front-end. This is
tabular RL's scaling wall, inherited intact. Neural hybrid nodes (S5) can push it
back but change the free-energy semantics at the boundary.

**H5. Planning is finite-horizon inference; policies are factorized.** LAIF's win
is linear-in-T policy inference, but T must be chosen, and a receding horizon is
myopic beyond it: payoffs more than T steps out exert zero pull. Further, the
control posterior factorizes per timestep (mean-field over u_t), so the agent
infers marginal action tendencies, not contingent plans ("if the cue says left,
go left" as a *policy tree*). Sophisticated-inference-style conditional planning
is outside this factorization; replanning every tick recovers much of it in
practice but is not the same object.

**H6. No convergence or optimality guarantees for GFE.** The GFE is non-convex;
Part II §4.5 documents that the naive fixed-point message diverges in cases, and
the Newton-solved variant still finds only local stationary points — Part II
Fig. 9's bimodal win histogram is the framework itself telling you agents
sometimes lock into bad optima depending on initialization. Expect and monitor
this; do not debug it as an implementation defect.

**H7. Conjugate continual learning has no principled forgetting.** Dirichlet
counts accumulate forever: the posterior sharpens monotonically, so a
nonstationary environment (the maze's reward statistics change at trial 500) is
absorbed ever more slowly. Exponential count decay / power priors fix this in
practice but are ad hoc — the "true Bayesian" semantics ends where the
environment stops being stationary. Relatedly, under model misspecification the
posterior converges confidently to the best wrong answer; the framework cannot
tell you your model class is wrong (low evidence hints at it; nothing repairs it).

**H8. Factors must have tractable local expectations.** Every node needs its
average energy and entropy contributions computable (closed form, quadrature, or
low-variance sampling) for the FE ledger to be exact. Factors without that —
arbitrary black-box likelihoods, implicit simulators — can only enter through
approximating surrogates, which reintroduces exactly the shortcut-taking the
project forbids.

**H9. Latent-state identifiability.** Learned latent categories are only defined
up to permutation (and sometimes merging) — the engine may learn a perfectly
predictive A matrix whose state labels mean nothing to a human. Interpretability
of learned structure is not provided by the math; it comes from priors and
constraints the modeler adds.

## Soft limitations

**S1. Message-rule coverage (the big one).** At completion we have: BP/VMP for
Cat/Dirichlet/equality/δ/transition-mixture, and GFE messages for the discrete
goal-observation composite. Everything else is a derivation ticket:
- *Gaussian/linear-Gaussian GFE messages* — genuinely open research: Koudahl 2021
  showed EFE in linear-Gaussian systems yields no purposeful exploration, so the
  continuous epistemic story is unresolved, not merely underived.
- *Nonlinear continuous factors* — need EP/moment-matching or sampling messages
  with controlled FE accounting.
- *Chance constraints, mixture/hierarchical continuous nodes* — flagged as future
  work by the papers themselves.
The registry architecture exists precisely so each of these lands as an isolated
contribution.

**S2. Importance-sampling noise in parameter messages.** The message to A is a
non-conjugate log-message evaluated by importance sampling; variance grows with
column dimensionality and makes the GFE trace stochastic (hence burn-in
averaging). Better estimators (Laplace approximation of the message, quadrature,
reparameterized control variates) are incremental research that would directly
improve learning stability.

**S3. Deep temporal / hierarchical models.** The papers say extensions are
"straightforward — write the CFFG," which is true of the *notation*; the message
rules for inter-level couplings (Cat parameters generated by a higher level,
temporal thickness à la de Vries & Friston 2017) still need deriving and testing.
Engineering plus modest derivation.

**S4. Contingent planning.** H5's policy factorization can be partially lifted:
structured (non-mean-field) constraints over control sequences, or explicit
branching on future observations, trade compute for policy expressiveness.
Receding-horizon replanning already recovers most practical value cheaply.

**S5. Neural hybrid nodes.** Deterministic NN factors with learned amortized
messages (extended-VMP style) are the known escape hatch from H4's tabular wall —
JAX makes the plumbing natural. Research-grade: the FE contribution of such nodes
is approximate, so they must be quarantined behind explicit "surrogate" bead
types to keep the exact-FE guarantee for the rest of the graph.

**S6. Structure search as an outer loop.** Free energy is a model-comparison
score, so propose-and-score topology search (add state, split factor, compare FE
on held-out rollouts) is buildable on top of the engine. Expensive but not novel
math.

**S7. Scale engineering.** Sparse A/B matrices, factored transition tensors,
GPU-resident arenas, incremental recompilation, smarter (residual) schedules —
ordinary optimization work, unbounded appetite.

**S8. Goal-specification ergonomics.** Goals are prior distributions over future
observations; translating task intent into calibrated `c` vectors (the softmax
utility dance) is modeler burden today. Goal hyperpriors (learned goals, Part II
§7.2) and a small goal-DSL would soften it.

## The one-paragraph honest summary

Completed, this is a *transparent, compositional, continually-learning
discrete world-model engine* with principled curiosity — exact free-energy
accounting, models you can read, edit, checkpoint, and glue. It will not do
representation learning, will not scale past modest discrete state spaces without
hand-factored structure, will not plan contingently beyond its horizon, and
inherits every classical caveat of loopy variational inference. Its natural
habitat: problems where the state ontology is designable (devices, protocols,
games, control loops, cognitive-model experiments), not problems where the
ontology must be learned from raw sensor streams.

Count decay works but is ad hoc — Bayesian purity ends where stationarity does. Related: under model misspecification the agent converges *confidently* to the best wrong answer and can't tell you.

8. **Factors need tractable local expectations.** Black-box likelihoods and implicit simulators can only enter through surrogates — which is exactly the shortcut-taking your brief forbids, so they're effectively out.

9. **Latent labels aren't identifiable.** A learned A matrix can be perfectly predictive with state labels that mean nothing to a human (permutation symmetry). Interpretability comes from priors you impose, not the math.

## Soft limitations — each one a future research or engineering ticket

1. **Message-rule coverage — the big one.** At v1 we'll have BP/VMP for Cat/Dirichlet/equality/δ/transition-mixture plus GFE messages for the discrete goal-observation composite. Everything else is a derivation: nonlinear continuous nodes, chance constraints, and especially **Gaussian GFE messages, which are open *research*, not just underived** — Koudahl 2021 showed EFE in linear-Gaussian systems produces no purposeful exploration, so the continuous epistemic story is genuinely unresolved in the field. The rule registry exists so each of these lands as an isolated contribution.

2. **Importance-sampling noise** in the message to A — variance grows with dimensionality; better estimators (Laplace, quadrature, control variates) would directly stabilize learning.

3. **Hierarchical/deep-temporal models** — the notation extends trivially, the inter-level message rules still need deriving and testing.

4. **Contingent planning** — structured constraints over control sequences can partially lift the factorized-policy limit, trading compute for expressiveness.

5. **Neural hybrid nodes** — the known escape hatch from the tabular wall, but their FE contributions are approximate, so they'd be quarantined behind explicit "surrogate" bead types to preserve the exact-FE guarantee elsewhere.

6. **Structure search as an outer loop** — FE is a model-comparison score, so propose-and-score topology search is buildable *around* the engine. Expensive, not novel math.

7. **Scale engineering** (sparse matrices, factored transitions, GPU arenas) and **goal-specification ergonomics** (the softmax utility dance for `c` vectors; goal hyperpriors soften it) — ordinary work, unbounded appetite.

**One-paragraph honest summary:** completed, this is a transparent, compositional, continually-learning *discrete world-model engine with principled curiosity* — exact free-energy accounting, models you can read, edit, checkpoint, glue, and ship as a ZIP. It won't learn representations, won't scale past modest hand-factored state spaces, won't plan contingently past its horizon, and inherits every classical caveat of loopy variational inference. Its natural habitat is problems where the state ontology is *designable* — devices, protocols, games, control loops, cognitive-model experiments — not ones where the ontology must be dug out of raw sensor streams.

None of these undermine the project; they mostly define its lane. Ready to start M0 (uv scaffold, tk epics for M1–M6, CI) whenever you say go.

- Sensor/actuator adapters are plain Python callbacks mapping env observations to
  one-hot data bindings and control marginals to env actions.

### 5b. Colony execution (many small graphs, one machine)

A first-class use case: ~10²–10³ small CFFG instances running concurrently as
adaptive components ("learning goo") inside a larger deterministic host system.
This costs three design constraints, adopted from M1 onward, and one extra layer —
not an architecture change:

- **Stateless engine, state as pytree.** An instance is pure data:
  `(structure_hash, params, messages, rng_key)`. The compiled step is a pure
  function `state → state`. No singletons, no Python object holding arrays.
  (JAX pushes us here anyway; we make it a contract.)
- **Batch axis by construction.** The compiled step must be `vmap`-compatible
  (no data-dependent Python control flow; Newton loops as `lax` primitives with
  fixed iteration caps). Then N instances *sharing a structure* execute as one
  batched XLA kernel — a colony of clones with different parameters, data, and
  RNG keys is barely more expensive than one instance.
- **Batching by structure hash.** The JIT cache is already keyed on structure;
  the colony scheduler groups instances by that key and runs one vmapped call
  per group per tick. A hundred goo blobs = (few unique templates) compiled
  kernels, not a hundred compilations.
- **`Colony` layer** above the agent runtime: owns the instance table, groups by
  structure, ticks groups (sync round-robin first; JAX's async dispatch already
  overlaps host code and XLA), routes host-system signals to instance data/goal
  ports and actions back. Inter-instance coupling happens **through the host via
  ports** (the Part II buyer/seller pattern: nested Markov blankets, exchanging
  observations/actions), never by merging graphs at runtime.

Known cost: per-instance *structure* evolution fragments the batching (each
divergent structure = its own compile). The goo pattern should draw structures
from a small template library and evolve parameters freely; structure variants
get promoted to the library deliberately, not mutated ad hoc. Memory is a
non-issue at this scale (a T-maze-sized instance's arenas are kilobytes).

## Session protocol (context hygiene)

This project will span many context windows. The rule that makes that survivable:
**tickets are the shared memory; the repo carries no session state.**

- **Start of session**: read this file, run `tk ready`, pick ONE ticket (or a few
  trivially small ones). Don't re-derive project state from scratch — the ticket's
  description, design notes, and comments are the handoff.
- **During**: atomic commits referencing the ticket ID. Discovered work becomes a
  *new ticket* (linked with a dependency), not scope drift in the current one.
- **End of session**: leave `main` green and the tree clean. Update the ticket with
  a handoff comment — what's done, what's next, any gotcha — then close it or leave
  it `in_progress` with that comment as the resume point. A session that ends with
  uncommitted work or an un-updated ticket has failed its landing.
- **One ticket ≈ one context window.** If a ticket can't fit, split it before
  starting, not after running out of context.

### Sub-agent research protocol

- Spawn research sub-agents with **specific questions**, not topics ("What update
  rule does PGMax use for factor-to-variable messages and how are its arenas
  indexed?" — not "read about PGMax").
- The sub-agent's report gets **distilled into the ticket that needed it** as a
  comment (question → answer → source → confidence). Durable engine-relevant
  conclusions go into docstrings next to the code they justify.
- Never paste a paper or long raw report into the main context; never let a
  sub-agent's full output become a new markdown file.

### Document policy

Exactly four canonical documents: `AGENTS.md` (rules), `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`
(design), `docs/LIMITATIONS.md` (scope honesty), `README.md` (once there's
something to run). **Update in place; do not create new markdown files.** Everything
else lives in tickets (state, decisions-in-progress, research findings), code
docstrings (durable knowledge), or tests (executable claims). If a decision changes
the architecture, edit ARCHITECTURE.md in the same commit as the change.

# AGENTS.md — Ground Rules for the CFFG Project

This repository implements **Constrained Forney-style Factor Graphs (CFFGs)** and
**Lagrangian Active Inference (LAIF)** in JAX, following:

- *Realising Synthetic Active Inference Agents, Part I: Epistemic Objectives and
  Graphical Specification Language* (Koudahl, van de Laar, de Vries — arXiv:2306.08014)
- *Part II: Variational Message Updates* (van de Laar, Koudahl, de Vries)

Both papers live in `notes/` (PDFs plus extracted text). The project brief is in the
Obsidian vault at `agents/CFFG/0.0.md`. Reference implementation for parity testing:
https://github.com/biaslab/LAIF (Julia/RxInfer).

## Rules

1. **Package management: `uv` only.** Use `uv init`, `uv add`, `uv run`, `uv sync`.
   Never call `pip` directly, never hand-edit lockfiles. The venv is managed by uv.

2. **Atomic git commits.** One logical change per commit — a commit should build and
   pass tests on its own. Commit early and often; keep refactors separate from
   behavior changes. Reference ticket IDs in commit messages (e.g. `tk-42: ...`).

3. **Tickets via `tk`.** All work is tracked in the `tk` ticket system (`tk --help`
   for usage). Break work into small tickets with dependency links, use epics for the
   major milestones, and close tickets in the same session as the commit that
   resolves them. Before starting work, check `tk` for ready tickets.

4. **Act autonomously.** The agent has broad access to this machine and should use
   it: run tests, install deps, create tickets, commit, and keep moving without
   asking for permission on routine steps. Ask only for genuinely irreversible or
   scope-changing decisions.

5. **Side research goes to sub-agents.** When background reading is needed
   (downloading another paper, checking how PGMax allocates tensors, clarifying an
   active-inference derivation), spawn a sub-agent with the *specific questions* to
   answer and have it report back a short summary. Do not read whole papers into the
   main context window mid-task.

## Technical invariants

- **True Bethe/Generalised free energy.** No shortcuts in the objective: free-energy
  evaluation must follow the papers' definitions (node-local BFE terms, edge-entropy
  overcounting corrections, P-substitution for GFE nodes). FE values are the
  convergence signal and the policy-scoring quantity — treat them as first-class
  outputs, and test them against analytically known cases.
- **Messages in log-space** wherever feasible; normalize aggressively; explicit JAX
  PRNG keys for anything stochastic (e.g. importance-sampled messages) so runs are
  reproducible.
- **Serialization is the source of truth.** Model structure lives in the template
  format (no large blobs inline — blobs are file paths); the compiled JAX arena is a
  derived artifact and must always be reconstructible from the template + data.

content.text:
Both answers are now enshrined and committed — colony execution in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` (§5b), the SOP in `AGENTS.md`. Here's the substance.

## Multi-graph outlook: the goo is not just feasible, it's nearly free — *if* we adopt three constraints now

The short answer: **a hundred small graphs is the happy path for this architecture, not a strain on it**, because JAX's functional style and the arena design already point there. No radical change — three design contracts adopted from M1, plus one thin layer:

1. **Stateless engine, state as pytree.** An instance is pure data — `(structure_hash, params, messages, rng_key)` — and the compiled step is a pure function `state → state`. No Python object owns arrays. JAX forces most of this anyway; we make it a contract so nobody sneaks in a singleton.

2. **Batch axis by construction.** If the compiled step is `vmap`-compatible (no data-dependent Python branching; Newton inner loops as `lax` primitives with fixed iteration caps), then N instances *sharing a structure* run as **one batched XLA kernel** with different parameters, data, and RNG keys per lane. A hundred T-maze-sized clones costs barely more than one — their message arenas are kilobytes each, and XLA eats the batch dimension for breakfast.

3. **Batching by structure hash.** The JIT cache is already keyed on structure. The colony scheduler groups instances by that key: a hundred goo blobs drawn from, say, five templates = five compiled kernels, five vmapped calls per tick. Compilation happens per *template*, never per *instance*.

On top sits a small **`Colony` layer**: instance table, group-and-tick loop, and routing between the host system's signals and each instance's data/goal ports. Importantly, **instances couple through the host via ports, never by merging graphs** — this is exactly the buyer/seller pattern from Part II (nested Markov blankets exchanging observations and actions), so the papers already validate the goo topology conceptually.

The one real cost to know about: **per-instance structure evolution fragments the batching.** If each blob mutates its own topology, every mutant needs its own compile and the vmap win evaporates. So the goo pattern should be: parameters evolve freely per instance (cheap, batched), structures come from a small deliberate template library, and new structural variants get *promoted* to the library rather than mutated ad hoc. Structure edits stay a slow, deliberate operation; parameter learning is the fast loop. That division happens to match the biology metaphor pretty well.

## Context hygiene SOP — now in AGENTS.md

Fully agree with your instinct: tickets over markdown. The enshrined protocol:

- **Tickets are the shared memory; the repo carries no session state.** Every session: `tk ready`, pick **one ticket** (one ticket ≈ one context window — split before starting if it won't fit), work in atomic commits referencing the ID, and land with a **handoff comment** on the ticket: what's done, what's next, gotchas. A session ending with a dirty tree or a stale ticket "failed its landing."
- **Discovered work becomes a new linked ticket**, never scope drift in the current one.
- **Sub-agent protocol:** spawn with *specific questions*, not topics; the report gets distilled into the ticket that needed it (question → answer → source → confidence); durable conclusions go into docstrings next to the code they justify. Sub-agent output never becomes a new markdown file and never gets pasted wholesale into the main context.
- **Hard cap of four canonical docs** — AGENTS.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, LIMITATIONS.md, and eventually README.md — all updated *in place*, in the same commit as the change they describe. Everything else lives in tickets, docstrings, or tests (executable claims beat prose).

One thing I'd add beyond what you asked: **"leave main green" is itself a context-hygiene rule.** The next context window's most expensive activity is figuring out whether the previous one left things broken. Green tests + clean tree + a handoff comment means each session cold-starts in minutes, and the ticket graph becomes the project's long-term memory — which is thematically appropriate, given what we're building.

Ready for M0 whenever you are: `uv init`, tk epics for M1–M6 with the colony constraints baked into M1's acceptance criteria, pytest + ruff.

    ".ruff_cache",
    "node_modules",
}


def test_no_contraband_markdown():
    found = {
        str(p.relative_to(REPO))
        for p in REPO.rglob("*.md")

    }
    contraband = sorted(found - CANONICAL_DOCS)

        "to defend that in review."
    )

    """The rule cuts both ways: the four documents must actually be there."""
    missing = sorted(d for d in CANONICAL_DOCS if not (REPO / d).is_file())
    assert not missing, f"Canonical documents missing: {missing}"

## Dependency policy (JAX ecosystem)

Adopt (well-established, matched to our actual needs):

- **`jax`** — the engine substrate.
- **`equinox`** — pytree containers for engine/instance state. `eqx.Module` gives
  typed dataclass-pytrees, and `filter_jit`/`filter_vmap` cleanly separate static
  fields (structure hash, shapes, schedule) from dynamic arrays (messages,
  parameters) — exactly our compile boundary. Used for *state containers and
  compiled callables*, not neural networks.
- **`jaxtyping`** — shape/dtype annotations on message-rule signatures, runtime
  checked in tests. Message-passing bugs are shape bugs; catch them at the rule
  boundary.
- **`chex`** — test assertions (pytree/shape equality, jit-vs-nojit variants).
- **`safetensors`** — parameter blobs in the `.cffgz` bundle.
- **`hypothesis`** — property tests (FE accounting invariants, normalization).

Explicitly not adopted (revisit only with a ticket making the case):

- **`flax`/NNX** — neural-network library; nothing here is a neural net until
  hybrid surrogate nodes (LIMITATIONS S5), and Equinox covers that day too.
- **`numpyro`/`blackjax`** — sampling-based inference; different paradigm, and
  leaning on it risks "shortcut" FE evaluation.
- **`distrax`/`tfp.substrates.jax`** — heavyweight for what Cat/Dirichlet need;
  `jax.scipy.special` (digamma, logsumexp) covers the math. Reconsider at the
  continuous milestone.
- **`pgmax`** — read for arena-layout ideas; BP-only scope makes it a dead-end
  dependency.
- **`optax`/`jaxopt`** — first-order optimizers; our Newton solves are a few
  lines of `jax.jacobian` + `lax.while_loop` on tiny systems.

One structural rule: **`cffg.core` (IR + serialization) imports neither JAX nor
Equinox.** Templates must be loadable, validatable, and editable on a machine
with no accelerator stack; JAX enters at the compiler boundary.

## Staging for hierarchical and sophisticated inference

- **Hierarchical models: cleanly additive, plan as M7.** Templates-with-ports
  already compose vertically: a higher level places priors on a lower level's
  parameters or goal statistics (Part II §7.2's goal hyperprior is the depth-2
  base case, and the buyer/seller simulation is two coupled models at different
  timescales). What M7 adds is message rules for inter-level couplings
  (Dirichlet hyperpriors exist; Cat-parameters-from-a-parent and temporal
  thickness à la de Vries & Friston 2017 need deriving) and nested-schedule
  support in the VM. No IR or compiler changes anticipated.
- **Sophisticated inference: shallow yes, deep no.** Contingent planning
  ("branch on what I might observe") can be expressed as a *bigger template* —
  observation-branch mixture nodes unrolled into a policy tree — so the engine
  runs it without architectural change; the cost is combinatorial in branch
  depth (practical to depth ~2–3). Deep SI is tree search, which is precisely
  what LAIF exists to avoid; it will not fall out of message passing
  (LIMITATIONS H5/S4). Default posture: receding-horizon replanning first,
  shallow branch templates where contingency demonstrably pays.

All three done — and the project now exists as a real uv package with its first passing (and verified-to-bite) test, first ticket opened and closed per our own SOP. Answers:

**Equinox: yes, and it's now policy.** It's exactly right for our stateless-pytree contract: `eqx.Module` gives typed dataclass-pytrees for engine state, and `filter_jit`/`filter_vmap` handle the static-vs-dynamic field split (structure hash and shapes static, messages and parameters dynamic) that *is* our compile boundary. We use it for state containers and compiled callables — not as a neural-net library. Alongside it I adopted `jaxtyping` (message-passing bugs are shape bugs; annotate every rule signature), `chex` (test assertions), `safetensors`, and `hypothesis`. Deliberately **not** adopted, with reasons recorded in ARCHITECTURE.md: flax (nothing here is a neural net until surrogate nodes), numpyro/blackjax (sampling paradigm — the "shortcut FE" temptation), distrax/TFP (heavyweight; `jax.scipy.special` covers Cat/Dirichlet math), pgmax (read for ideas, dead-end as a dependency), optax/jaxopt (our Newton solves are a few lines on tiny systems). One structural rule worth highlighting: **`cffg.core` imports neither JAX nor Equinox** — templates must load and validate on a machine with no accelerator stack; JAX enters at the compiler.

**The contraband test is in and armed.** `tests/test_hygiene.py` fails the build if any markdown exists outside the four canonical docs — with one delicious discovery: `tk` stores tickets *as markdown* in `.tickets/`, so the ticket pile is the one sanctioned exemption, right there in the test with a comment saying so. I verified it actually catches a planted `docs/SCRATCH.md` before trusting it, and there's a companion test asserting the four canonical docs *exist* (the rule cuts both ways). The failure message tells the offender where their content actually belongs.

**Hierarchical and sophisticated inference — one clean yes, one honest split:**

- **Hierarchical: cleanly additive, now staged as M7.** Templates-with-ports already compose vertically — a higher level placing priors on a lower level's parameters or goals is just composition, and the papers already demonstrate the base cases (the goal hyperprior in Part II §7.2 is depth-2 hierarchy; buyer/seller is two coupled models at different timescales). M7's real work is deriving the inter-level message rules and adding nested-schedule support. No IR or compiler changes anticipated.
- **Sophisticated inference: shallow yes, deep no.** Contingent plans ("branch on what I might observe") can be expressed as a *bigger template* — observation-branch mixture nodes unrolled into a policy tree — and the engine runs that without any architectural change. But the cost is combinatorial in branch depth (practical to ~2–3), and that's not an implementation gap: deep SI *is* tree search, which is precisely the thing LAIF exists to replace. It will never fall out of message passing. Default posture: receding-horizon replanning first, shallow branch templates where contingency demonstrably pays.
